evidence.claim: The Governor Casey Byway follows a four-lane freeway between Carbondale Township and Dunmore, with forested stretches beside Lackawanna County's developed communities.
evidence.quote: The freeway continues northeast through forests as it bypasses Carbondale to the east, with a westbound scenic overlook.

evidence.claim: The Moosic Mountains lie east of the highway.

evidence.claim: VisitPA highlights access to Steamtown National Historic Site, the Pennsylvania Anthracite Heritage Museum and the Lackawanna Coal Mine.
evidence.quote: The byway provides access to historical sites including Steamtown National Historic Site, the Pennsylvania Anthracite Heritage Museum, and the Lackawanna Coal Mine.

evidence.claim: U.S. 6 did not always reach Carbondale through Scranton.
evidence.quote: US 6 also used present PA 706, US 11, and PA 106 between Wyalusing and Carbondale, while US 106 took the southerly route via Scranton.

evidence.claim: By the end of 1927 it had exchanged routes with U.S. 106, taking the southern route through Scranton.
evidence.quote: By the end of 1927, US 6 had replaced US 120 in running west from Kane to Erie (making US 120 no longer connect to its "parent" US 20) and had swapped places with US 106 via Scranton

evidence.claim: The modern freeway bypasses Carbondale to the east, while Business Route 6 runs through town on Main Street.
evidence.quote: U.S. Business Route 6 runs down Main Street, Carbondale, as the main highway through the city.

evidence.claim: The byway designation came under Act 33 of 2003.
evidence.quote: HB 1549, Act 33, Session of 2003, Enacted November 6, 2003.

evidence.claim: Carbondale grew with anthracite mining on land developed by William and Maurice Wurts, founders of the Delaware and Hudson Canal Company.
evidence.quote: The land area that became Carbondale was developed by William and Maurice Wurts, the founders of the Delaware and Hudson Canal Company, during the rise of the anthracite coal mining industry in the early 19th century.

evidence.claim: In 1899, Dr. Matthew J. Shields taught 25 miners from the Jermyn Coal Colliery how to treat injured colleagues before a physician could reach the mine.
evidence.quote: In 1899, Dr. Matthew J. Shields conducted the nation's first training class on First Aid at the Windsor Hotel. He instructed 25 miners from the Jermyn Coal Colliery how to provide quick, effective medical care until a physician could reach the mine.

evidence.claim: The class met at the Windsor Hotel.
evidence.quote: at the Windsor Hotel.

evidence.claim: Jermyn's early twentieth-century industries also included cut glass, silk, powder, sawmills and bottling works.
evidence.quote: Coal mines, cut glass works, silk, powder, grist, planing, sawmills, bottling works, and fertilizer factories dotted the borough during the early years of the twentieth century.

evidence.claim: The borough stands on the Lackawanna River and bears the name of John Jermyn, a mining businessman.
evidence.quote: The borough originally named Gibsonburg, was named for John Jermyn, a businessperson in the mining industry.

evidence.claim: The borough stands on the Lackawanna River
evidence.quote: Located on the Lackawanna River

evidence.claim: The 38-foot-deep Archbald Pothole cuts through sandstone, shale and coal.
evidence.quote: Archbald Pothole is 38 feet (11.6 m) deep and 42 feet (12.8 m) wide at its maximum diameter. The pothole cuts through layers of sandstone, shale and coal.

evidence.claim: Miner Patrick Mahon uncovered it in 1884 while extending a shaft.
evidence.quote: A coal miner, Patrick Mahon, discovered Archbald Pothole in 1884. Mahon was extending a mine shaft.

evidence.claim: His blast released water and stones into the workings, and the miners fled.
evidence.quote: When he set off a blast of explosives, water and stones came pouring into the mine shaft. He and the other miners fled the scene fearing for their lives.

evidence.claim: Almost 1,000 tons of rounded stones were removed before manager Edward Jones recognized the opening as a pothole.
evidence.quote: Almost 1,000 tons of small rounded stones were removed and Jones soon realized that the vertical tunnel discovered by the coal miners was a large pothole.

evidence.claim: It first served as a mine ventilation shaft, then became a tourist attraction.
evidence.quote: After serving as a ventilation shaft for the mine, the pothole was fenced in by the owner of the land, Colonel Hackley, for tourists.

evidence.claim: The state park, on Business Route 6, formally opened in 1964.
evidence.quote: Archbald Pothole State Park was formally opened in 1964.

evidence.claim: The pothole cuts through layers of sandstone, shale and coal.
evidence.quote: The pothole cuts through layers of sandstone, shale and coal.

evidence.claim: on Business Route 6
evidence.quote: Archbald Pothole State Park is on U.S. Route 6 Business in the borough of Archbald.

evidence.claim: Its Romanesque design includes a large semicircular entrance, with turrets of rusticated stone and brick.
evidence.quote: It features a massive, half-circle primary entrance and rusticated stone and brick turrets.

evidence.claim: Its Romanesque design
evidence.quote: in the  Romanesque-style.

evidence.claim: Glacial meltwater formed the hole; its elliptical opening narrows downward, from 42 by 24 feet to 17 by 14 feet at the bottom.
evidence.quote: The pothole is 38 feet (12 m) deep and has an elliptical shape. The diameter of the pothole decreases downward. The largest diameter is 42 feet (13 m) by 24 feet (7.3 m). At the bottom it is 17 feet (5.2 m) by 14 feet (4.3 m).

evidence.claim: Glacial meltwater formed the hole
evidence.quote: Potholes are also formed by the action of glacial meltwater. Archbald Pothole is an example of just such a pothole.

evidence.quote: US 6 also used present PA 706, US 11, and PA 106 between Wyalusing and Carbondale, while US 106 took the southerly route via Scranton.

evidence.quote: As approved by the American Association of State Highway Officials (AASHO) on November 11, 1926

flags: PennDOT defines the byway from I-81 in Dunmore to Business Route 6 in Carbondale Township; VisitPA and the U.S. 6 article end it at PA 247 in Jessup. Used PennDOT as the designation authority.
Driving order follows material from Carbondale toward Dunmore, reversing the current narrative. Jermyn is added between Carbondale and Archbald; existing moment titles and coordinates are retained.
Cache lacks the freeway construction date, builders and campaigning history. Overview distinguishes the 1927 U.S. 6 rerouting from the later freeway and 2004 byway designation.
The current mine-fire date range was omitted: the dedicated cache article alternates 1943/1946 starts and containment/extinguishment in 1972/1974. No unsupported claim of a present fire is made.
Jermyn first-aid instruction is supported only by secondary text; omitted the national-first claim and unquantified injury-reduction claim. No surviving hotel or access claim is made.
Jermyn is shorter than 90 words: the cache supports a compact account of the miners' first-aid class but no surviving place to visit or current local practice.
